key_gap: Both sides converged on the same verdict (2-week incident→change-class feedback pipeline + canary rule for the 5 recurring classes; defer the 25 hires; ≈30% incident cut, SLO ≥ 99.9% in 2 quarters), but the human saw it at first sight: it mapped the reinforcing firefighting loop and the headcount inflow loop, positioned candidates on the full leverage scale (parameters → delays → negative-feedback strength → information flows → rules → goals), and ranked by change-per-effort in one pass — including the non-obvious read that hiring is near-bottom leverage (a number change inside unchanged loop structure). The AI opened sympathetic to the board's capacity frame, reached the same conclusion only through explicit effort math and natural-experiment evidence (18 hires → SLO flat), and spent a pass re-deriving what the loop map gives immediately.
learning_signal: For org reliability and policy problems, leverage is decided by loop structure, not by where the pressure appears: first map the governing feedback loops (page → context switch → hasty change → page) and ask of every candidate 'does it add load to the loop or break it?'; then position intervention points on the leverage scale — information flows (adding a missing link in the feedback path, e.g., aggregating incident tags) and rules (a canary mandate) beat parameters (headcount) by orders of magnitude, and a ~2-week information-flow build can make the rule lever aimable. Failed prior initiatives are natural experiments — read them before proposing anything.
suggested_improvement: Add a 'leverage pre-screen' to WHAT for org/policy and reliability problems: (a) map the governing feedback loops and state whether each candidate intervention feeds or breaks them; (b) position candidates on a leverage scale (parameters < delays < negative-feedback strength < information flows < rules < goals); (c) before any 'add capacity' candidate, cite the natural-experiment evidence from prior similar additions; (d) require the change-per-effort ranking before HOW. This converts the AI's correct-but-late convergence into first-pass insight.

key_gap: The pure style misidentified leverage (its registry weakness). It pre-committed to structural levers: framed the funnel drop as surface behavior of the growth-org incentive system, ranked a $500k/6-month goals/KPI transformation program as the deep fix, ranked the observed cause (checkout regression) as 'low leverage — patching a symptom changes no loop,' and dismissed the deployment-window correlation as coincidence — without ever opening the funnel data (100% of the drop at the payment step) or the deploy log (3-week onset matches the API upgrade). The AI localized the drop to the funnel step and window, ran the cheap decisive test (roll back → conversion returns), and picked the 1-hour fix restoring ≈ $1.2M/month; the 'deep' lever had no window-tied evidence and no falsifier and was rejected on parsimony.
learning_signal: Leverage is defined by change per effort along the causal chain, not by structural depth: when a candidate (a) fully localizes the symptom (funnel step), (b) matches its onset window, and (c) is verifiable by a cheap decisive test, it outranks unfalsifiable structural stories regardless of how 'deep' they look — the boring direct fix is often the true leverage point (small shift, large change). Deep-looking levers (goals, rules, culture) must be gated on evidence tied to the symptom's onset before being ranked; a mechanism unchanged for years cannot explain a 3-week spike.
suggested_improvement: Add a 'leverage verification gate' in WHY for diagnosis tasks: every high-ranked lever must (a) state the observable that would falsify it, (b) account for the symptom's onset window and localization (funnel/deploy log), and (c) be compared on change-per-effort against the cheapest candidate that fully explains the data — with the boring direct fix explicitly ranked before any structural program. Reject levers whose evidence is unfalsifiable or untimed.
